<jats:p><p>This paper examines the mechanisms of automatic trading platforms in cryptocurrency and Contract for Difference (CFD) markets and evaluates whether existing human oversight frameworks are adequate to protect retail investors. Drawing on regulatory frameworks, empirical case analysis, and academic literature, it is argued that AI at many retail trading platforms functions primarily as a client acquisition engine rather than a trading improvement tool — a distinction with profound implications for investor protection and regulatory design. The paper analyses the structural conflict of interest inherent in the CFD market-maker model, the 'black box' problem that undermines regulatory oversight, and the specific regulatory exposure created by algorithmically optimised client targeting under the FCA's Consumer Duty framework. The paper demonstrates that existing oversight is systematically inadequate and proposes five policy reforms: mandatory algorithmic auditing, structural separation of market-making and advisory functions, explicit Consumer Duty guidance on AI acquisition models, enhanced international coordination for cryptocurrency markets, and improved retail investor dispute resolution mechanisms.</p>
<p>&nbsp;</p></jats:p>
title: A Study of Algorithmic Transparency, Regulatory Gaps, and Retail Investor Protection in Crypto and CFD Markets

title: 4.2. Regulatory barriers in the retail business
Should Retail Investors' Leverage Be Limited?

items.abstract: <jats:p>Does the provision of leverage to retail traders improve market quality or facilitate socially inefficient speculation that enriches financial intermediaries? This paper evaluates the effects of 2010 regulations that cap the provision of leverage to previously unregulated U.S. retail traders of foreign exchange. Using three unique data sets and a difference-in-differences approach, we document that the leverage constraint reduces trading volume by 23 percent, improves high-leverage traders' portfolio return by 18 percentage points per month (thereby alleviating their losses by 40 percent), and reduces brokerages' operating capital by 25 percent. Yet, the policy does not affect the relative bid-ask prices charged by the brokerages. The announcement of pending leverage restrictions has no effect on the traders or the market. We reconcile these findings with a model in which traders with heterogeneous and dogmatic beliefs take speculative positions in pursuit of high returns, and a competitive brokerage sector intermediates these trades subject to technological and informational costs. The model is largely consistent with our empirical findings, and it suggests that the leverage constraint policy generates a sizable belief-neutral improvement in social welfare by economizing on the productive resources used to intermediate speculation.</jats:p>
title: Should Retail Investors' Leverage Be Limited?

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Can retail-investor leverage predict aggregate market reversals? This paper examines this question using daily margin-financing and market-index data from Taiwan, a retail-investor-dominated equity market. Using TEJ data from January 1991 to May 2026, I construct market-wide overheating indicators from the TAIEX, aggregate margin balances, trading value, the short-selling-to-margin-financing ratio, and the account maintenance ratio. The baseline measure scales aggregate margin balances by the TAIEX level, capturing the extent to which leveraged retail participation is elevated relative to the market level. I then develop additional indicators that capture margin-chasing behavior, margin crowding relative to market liquidity, speculative exhaustion, and high-maintenance complacency. These components are combined into a composite overheating index designed to summarize broad-based retail-leverage overheating. 
<br>
<br>
 The empirical design identifies overheating episodes using rolling three-year percentile thresholds that rely only on information available up to the previous trading day. This approach avoids fixed nominal thresholds and mitigates look-ahead bias. Preliminary visual evidence shows that extreme readings of the composite overheating index often arise near major market peaks and periods of subsequent market weakness. The findings suggest that aggregate margin-financing conditions contain useful information about market fragility and reversal risk. More broadly, the paper highlights the role of retail-investor leverage in shaping aggregate return dynamics in equity markets with active individual-investor participation.</jats:p>
title: Retail Leverage, Margin-Financing Overheating, and Market Reversal Predictability
